theory.intro: Many real situations follow a non-linear relationship. A projectile's height traces a parabola, and a business's income can rise then fall. Reading these graphs — and finding where two graphs cross — answers practical questions like the greatest height, the break-even point, or when a target value is reached.
facts: The **maximum** or **minimum** of a quadratic model is read from the **vertex** (turning point) of its parabola.
A value of the model at a given input is read straight up from the horizontal axis to the curve, then across to the vertical axis (and vice-versa to find an input for a given output).
Two relationships are equal where their graphs **cross**; reading the crossing point solves the pair of simultaneous equations graphically.
In context, only part of a graph is usually sensible: time and physical quantities cannot be negative, so the model applies on a restricted domain.
steps: Identify what feature answers the question: a turning point, an intercept, a read-off value, or a crossing point.
Read the required coordinate(s) from the graph.
State the answer in the words of the context.

foundation.solution_text:
Time cannot be negative, so the part with $t<0$ has no meaning.
Once the ball hits the ground (near $t=4$) its height cannot go below $0$, so the part where the curve dips under the $t$-axis has no meaning.
Only the arc from release to landing, $0\le t\le4$, models the flight.

development.solution_text:
At the crossing point the two graphs have the same height.
So at $x=5$ (that is, $50$ meals) the income equals the cost, each $\$900$.
This is the break-even point: below it the van makes a loss, above it (until the curves cross again) it makes a profit.

Time cannot be negative, so the part with $t<0$ has no meaning.
The diver enters the water when $h=0$, at $t=3$; after that the model would give negative heights, which are below the water surface.
So only the arc with $0\le t\le3$ models the dive, from the board at $15$ m down to the water.
